pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
Docket No. AD26-7-000
 
PRE-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT OF  
STEVEN LIEBERMAN ON BEHALF OF  
AMERICAN MUNICIPAL POWER, INC. 
 
I appreciate the opportunity to participate in the upcoming Federal Energy 
Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) technical conference scheduled for 
July 23, 2026, as a panelist on Panel 2, titled “PJM Stakeholder Process – Design, 
Transparency, and Decision-Making.” This pre-technical conference statement, 
presented on behalf of American Municipal Power, Inc. (“AMP”), focuses on the subject 
matter of that panel discussion, as described in the Commission’s notice.1 
As Vice President of Transmission & Regulatory Affairs, I provide oversight and 
take responsibility for AMP’s advocacy in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, 
Inc. (“MISO”) and PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) RTO stakeholder processes, along 
with AMP’s participation in the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) 
standards development process. I hold a Bachelor of Arts degree in Environmental 
Science from Boston University. 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
These comments share the perspective of AMP as a non-profit public power 
wholesale supplier of electricity for 135 public power communities located across nine 
states, including seven PJM states. AMP’s member systems serve approximately 
 
1  See Second Supplemental Notice of Commission-Led Technical Conference, Docket No. AD26-7-000, 
at 4-6 (July 2, 2026).

2 
650,000 meters, and while AMP represents many of the larger public power systems in 
PJM, the average AMP member community is less than 5,000 meters and rural. Our 
member officials are keenly aware of the impact of PJM policies and governance on their 
local operations and costs for their customers. But AMP’s advocacy is not biased towards 
pricing outcomes. Said differently, AMP does not advocate for rules that are motivated to 
intentionally raise prices or lower prices. Instead, AMP advocates for sustainable, 
commonsense rules that will protect end-use customers from degraded reliability, while 
ensuring affordability. 
PJM’s existing governance framework generally works well and does not require 
major structural reform. The current sector-weighted voting process appropriately 
balances consensus-building with timely decision-making and ensures that significant 
proposals receive broad stakeholder support before advancing. 
AMP’s primary recommendation is to improve coordination and consistency 
between voting at senior committees and voting at lower-level committees, where voting 
results often determine which proposals move forward. AMP believes coordination 
between voting results at lower-level committees and votes taken by senior committees 
would strengthen stakeholder confidence, improve consensus-building, and make 
decision-making more efficient. 
Stakeholder representation and committee structure are not the source of delays. 
States and other interested parties appropriately have multiple opportunities to participate 
in PJM processes, and the speed of decision-making is largely determined by PJM’s 
prioritization of issues and meeting schedules. Accordingly, better issue prioritization is 
needed, rather than changes to stakeholder representation or governance.

3 
PJM’s most significant challenge remains resource adequacy and reliability, but 
the existing governance framework, with the adjustments proposed below, is sufficient to 
address those concerns and there is no basis for weakening stakeholder processes or 
reducing stakeholder input. Expanded use of expedited stakeholder procedures may 
result in compressed timelines that hinder stakeholder collaboration, reduce opportunities 
to build consensus, and create greater regulatory uncertainty. Better outcomes result 
when stakeholders have adequate time to develop and refine proposals. 
Finally, PJM should enhance transparency at the Board level. Adopting practices 
similar to those used by other regional transmission organizations, such as providing 
greater public access to Board meetings, agendas, and materials, would improve 
accountability and stakeholder confidence. Overall, AMP supports targeted transparency 
improvements while preserving the consensus-based processes that have historically 
promoted reliable and affordable electric service. 
II. 
COMMENTS 
Question 1: Sector-weighted Voting  
 
Do sector-weighted voting and existing voting thresholds strike the right balance 
between achieving consensus and taking timely action? 
 
Sector weighted voting (SWV) is used for votes of the Members Committee (MC) 
and the Markets and Reliability Committee (MRC) (i.e., the Senior Standing Committees). 
SWV and the related voting thresholds for issues to be deemed approved (or endorsed) 
achieves a reasonable balance between developing consensus and timely action. The 
threshold is two-thirds support from the five sectors, in which each sector provides 1.000 
votes towards the total. Thus the threshold for an issue to be deemed approved or passed 
via SWV is 3.334 (rounding up).

4 
PJM facilitates nearly all stakeholder meetings except for the MC and the Liaison 
Committee (LC). There is no voting at the LC, thus there is only one instance in which a 
PJM Member facilitates a committee in which voting occurs (the MC). In terms of timely 
action, the committee or task force facilitator or a stakeholder can “call the question” on 
an agenda item to ensure timely action. 
Achieving consensus does not mean unanimous support. In some instances, 
consensus is a simple majority threshold and in others it is a super-majority. While it may 
seem difficult to achieve a super-majority threshold, particularly on contentious issues, 
when it is attained, it signals to FERC that the proposal before it is supported by a broad 
range of PJM Members. 
Question 2. Transparency Reforms 
 
What transparency reforms would improve the quality of PJM’s stakeholder 
process and increase stakeholder confidence in its decision-making?  
 
Transparency reforms are desperately needed, particularly for matters of 
significance that come before the PJM Board following stakeholder consideration and that 
result in FERC filings. There is substantial opaqueness in the PJM Board’s deliberations 
on such matters. One aspect that PJM should consider adopting from SPP is that “[a]ll 
SPP Board meetings that are not in executive session are open to the public. All meeting 
materials, agendas, and minutes are publicly posted on the SPP website.”2 Transparency 
is key, recognizing that certain issues necessarily lend themselves to being discussed in 
executive session. 
 
2  See FERC, An Introductory Guide for Participation in Southwest Power Pool Processes (“Q. How is 
SPP Governed?”), https://www.ferc.gov/introductory-guide-participation-southwest-power-pool-
processes.

5 
MISO’s similarly open approach is also instructive. The MISO Board holds an open 
meeting each quarter. The committees of the Board hold open meetings at least each 
quarter. Stakeholders and the public are allowed to listen to these meetings. The Board 
and its committees cover general materials in open session, but do have executive 
sessions for material related to confidential business (personnel matters, legal matters, 
contract issues, etc.).  The committees publish and review a work plan for the year 
showing when they have open meetings and executive sessions with a general overview 
of the topics to be covered in the meetings.   
At the end of their meetings the MISO Board and its committees allow an 
opportunity for public comment. During MISO’s Board week, when the Board holds an 
open meeting, the Board joins the MISO Advisory Committee (AC)—the stakeholder 
committee with representatives from all of the stakeholder sectors—to hold a discussion 
on a topic decided prior to the meeting. The discussion for June 2026 was “Maintaining 
Resource Adequacy in a Time of Transition.” The MISO Board and the AC receive reports 
from the chairs of various MISO stakeholder groups.  After each report on the topics of 
interest being discussed at the stakeholder committees, the MISO Board and the AC have 
an opportunity to ask the chair of each group questions about the work of the committee. 
Additional opportunities for the PJM Board to interact with stakeholders and for 
stakeholders to hear PJM Board deliberations and understand the basis for decision-
making, more like other RTOs, could increase stakeholder confidence in, or at least 
understanding of, PJM Board decisions.

6 
Question 3. State Participation  
 
Are there structured opportunities in the stakeholder process for state 
participation (e.g., defined consultation windows, joint technical sessions) to 
provide input on topics that are of interest to the states? 
 
Yes, state participation is possible, and states (some perhaps more than others) 
do participate in stakeholder meetings, including by presenting proposals for 
consideration. Per Manual 34, Section 4: Roles and Responsibilities, “[t]here are several 
types of participants in the PJM stakeholder process, including the Members, PJM (the 
Office of the Interconnection, or Staff), the Independent Market Monitor (IMM) and the 
Organization of PJM States, Inc. and its member regulatory agencies. Additionally from 
time to time other parties may participate in the PJM stakeholder process.”3  
Section 4.1 Members and Other Participants, explains that “[i]t is the responsibility 
of each participant in the PJM stakeholder process to represent its interests in 
cooperation with all other stakeholders to ensure the reliability of the PJM system and 
implementation of efficient, fair and transparent markets.” Specifically, participant 
responsibility includes five stated items: 
• 
Articulating their interests, concerns, ideas and their basis of support for a 
particular approach or proposal; 
• 
Raising objections and concerns, and the responsibility to provide an alternative 
if they are not able to agree with a proposal or option; 
• 
Alerting the stakeholder meeting facilitator to specific sensitive concerns related 
to the process or subject matter; 
• 
Providing all materials in a timely manner for website posting and notification; 
and 
 
3  Additional information about the roles and responsibilities of the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) 
and State Regulators is provided in PJM, Manual 34, Section 4.4, at 23, https://www.pjm.com/-
/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m34.pdf.

7 
• 
Adhering to the Stakeholder Group’s Charter and work plan, and seeking to 
complete it in a timely and efficient manner that meets any regulatory or other 
deadlines. 
Moreover, PJM’s stakeholder process allows for the formation of a “user group.” 
Recently, the consumer advocates created a user group, the Affordability and Reliability 
for Residential Consumers User Group. The consumer advocates also joined with 
environmental interests to form the Public Interest & Environmental Organizations User 
Group. There is also the Independent State Agencies Committee (ISAC), which is a 
voluntary, stand-alone committee that consists of members from regulatory and other 
state agencies representing all of the states within the service territory of PJM and the 
District of Columbia. “The ISAC is an independent committee that shall not be controlled 
or directed by PJM or the PJM Board of Managers.”4 The ISAC provides “PJM with input 
to inform the assumptions, scenarios, and studies developed as part of PJM’s Regional 
Transmission Expansion Planning Protocol as well as to discuss alternative sensitivity 
studies, modeling assumptions, and scenario analyses.”5 The ISAC may also address 
“items described in section 1.5 of Schedule 6 of the PJM Operating Agreement,”6 i.e., the 
procedures for developing the PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Plan. 
Finally, one of the most direct ways any stakeholder may communicate its position 
is to send a letter to PJM’s President and CEO, and to PJM’s Board of Managers. States, 
public utility commissions, concerned citizens, and Members from every sector all avail 
themselves of this opportunity, which typically results in a timely response from the Board 
 
4  OPSI, ISAC Charter at 1, https://opsi.us/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/ISAC-Charter.pdf. 
5  Id.  
6  Id.

8 
Chair. A list of communications submitted to PJM and the responses from PJM are 
publicly posted on PJM.com here. 
Question 4. Governing Documents 
 
Do existing governing document provisions (e.g., Operating Agreement, Manuals) 
impede stakeholder decision-making and what changes could be made to 
address them? 
 
Although the current PJM governance framework remains generally sound, there 
are targeted reforms that could be made to improve the efficiency of the stakeholder 
process. Existing provisions of Manual 34 (PJM Stakeholder Process) impede 
stakeholder decision-making and a key example is the impact of voting that occurs at the 
“lower level” committees in determining which proposals may be voted on in the senior 
committees. The lower-level committees should play a critical role in screening and 
developing the proposals that are ultimately considered by the senior committees. For 
proposals to be viable, their ultimate approval at the Members Committee should be 
reasonably foreseeable by the lower-level committees. In order to efficiently build 
proposals that may achieve consensus at the critical Members Committee, it is imperative 
to ensure that the voting structure at the lower level Standing Committees adequately 
captures the views of stakeholders represented in MC voting. Under the existing rules, it 
does not. 
The current process impedes stakeholder decision-making because at the lower-
level committees, all PJM Members receive one vote, including Affiliates, but at the senior 
committees, each corporate family receives only one vote.  As a result, Members with 
more Affiliates control the flow of proposals from the lower-level committees to the senior 
committees, meaning that proposals that are not viable at the senior-level committees

9 
because there was not buy-in across the stakeholder sectors in the lower-level 
committees are sometimes moved forward, and potentially viable proposals are left 
behind. 
In this regard, the code of conduct included in Manual 34 explains that: 
the stakeholder process has been designed intentionally so 
that the decision-making authority is exclusively vested with 
the Senior Standing Committees consistent with Operating 
Agreement, section 8.4. Votes at the "lower" Standing 
Committees (e.g. the Operating Committee, Planning 
Committee, Market Implementation Committee, and Risk 
Management 
Committee) 
and 
their 
subordinate 
subcommittees and task forces have no such weight or finality 
in their votes. Votes at the lower level Standing Committees 
merely set the order of voting on various proposals that were 
considered in the lower Committee for consideration at the 
Senior Standing Committees and afford Members an 
opportunity to understand general stakeholder sentiment 
helpful in fostering further consensus building activities. See 
generally, Section 3: Purpose of the Stakeholder Process as 
well as Section 8: Consensus Based Issue Resolution at the 
Standing Committee Level. A PJM Members Committee vote 
is singularly the vote that fulfills their Operating Agreement 
responsibilities. All other Member votes and stakeholder polls 
are only indicative of a Members' preference or interest as 
solutions are explored.7 
At the two senior committees, the MRC and the MC, only Members are able to 
vote (i.e., no Affiliates and no non-Members). For all other committees and senior task 
forces, each Member gets one vote. The standard process for a Member seeking action 
on an item by the MRC and MC requires that the proposal first receive simple majority 
support at the subordinate, lower level committees and task forces. If multiple proposals 
achieve simple majority support, the proposal with the greatest level of support is deemed 
 
7  PJM, Manual 34, Section 4.5, at 23.

10 
the “main motion” and the others are “alternates.” If the main motion passes at the MRC 
and MC, there is no vote on the alternates.  
Thus the disparity in voting participants at the lower level compared to the senior 
level committees may and often does greatly impact the voting outcome at the MRC and 
MC. This is because a Member with multiple Affiliates has an outsized opportunity to 
influence the order of voting, and therefore the proposals that are voted on, at the senior 
level. The largest numbers of Affiliates belong to Members in the Generation Owner (260), 
Other Supplier (228), and Transmission Owner (39) sectors.8 Members in sectors 
typically viewed as aligned with consumer interests have few, if any, Affiliates; sector 
totals are: Electric Distributors (9); End Use Customers (4). 
Manual 34 explains that voting at the Standing Committees includes both Members 
and Affiliates, and that if a simple majority prefers a proposal over the status quo the 
proposal with the greatest level of support will become the Main Motion for consideration 
at the MRC, while other proposals will be Alternate Motions. If the Main Motion passes, 
no vote is taken on Alternate Motions.  
The status quo voting paradigm that allows Affiliates to vote at Standing 
Committees favors Members with registered Affiliates. The more Affiliates a Member has, 
and the more Affiliates a sector has, the greater the influence that Member and that sector 
have on Senior Standing Committees such as the MRC and MC, where voting is 
Members-only. Members who have substantial numbers of Affiliates are positioned to act 
as a veto on proposals that would otherwise be brought to the MRC for a vote by only 
Members (i.e., no Affiliates) since there are more Affiliate members in PJM (540) than 
 
8  PJM, Member List (July 10, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/about-pjm/member-services/member-list.

11 
voting Members (517).9 Due to their combined size, Members with their Affiliates may 
have a voting block with substantial sway over the voting results at the lower committees 
and, by implication, at the Senior Standing Committee level. As noted above, there are 
three sectors that have the overwhelming majority of total Affiliates in PJM and these 
three sectors, or a combination of any two of the three sectors, are able to determine 
which, if any, proposals may be voted on at the MRC by all five sectors. 
One simple way to fix this would be to modify the lower-level committee voting 
structure to match the senior committees. This would allow voting Members to better 
understand whether a proposal that is supported at a lower-level committee has sufficient 
sector weighted support to potentially pass an MC vote, and if not, to identify the sticking 
points so they can be addressed. 
Alternatively, in order to ensure that all Members of the MRC have the ability to act 
on any proposal voted on at the Standing Committee in an equal manner to the Main 
Motion, not just those preferred by two or three sectors with the vast majority of Affiliates, 
PJM should analyze the voting results of the Standing Committee. If a proposal has 
received support from at least one voting Member from four of the five sectors it should 
be viewed as a potentially viable proposal for consideration by the MRC. Voting on this 
additional proposal along with the proposal that received the greatest level of support 
above the simple-majority threshold would occur in a non-truncated manner, allowing 
both proposals to be voted on at the MRC simultaneously. If multiple proposals receive 
support from at least four of the five sectors, the proposal with the greatest number of 
 
9  Id.

12 
combined votes would be moved for consideration to the MRC along with the status quo 
“Main Motion” proposal.  
A proposal that receives support from at least one Member in four sectors would 
be deemed a viable proposal for the MRC to consider as it could pass the MRC even if 
one entire sector opposes it. This sensible change to the voting methodology for 
proposals considered by the MRC would mitigate any perceived veto power at either the 
Standing Committee level or the Senior Standing Committee level. 
Question 5. Stakeholder Process Reforms 
 
What reforms to the stakeholder process could ensure PJM can meet the region’s 
challenges? 
 
The single biggest challenge PJM continually faces is how to conduct a capacity 
auction to ensure sufficient quantities of capacity are available to meet anticipated 
demand plus adequate reserves to maintain a 1-in-10 level of reliability, consistent with 
the FERC-approved Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) capacity construct rules. RPM’s 
structure is contained within PJM’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT or Tariff). 
PJM has Federal Power Act section 205 filing rights over the OATT.10 No changes are 
needed to the stakeholder process to ensure PJM can meet the region’s resource 
adequacy challenges, given the section 205 filing rights that PJM currently enjoys over 
the terms and conditions of RPM. Rather than reforming the stakeholder process, 
significant reforms to how PJM prioritizes and schedules meetings to address the 
challenges should be made.  PJM already has the ability to do so but has not.   
 
10  With the exception of certain rights reserved by the Transmission Owners.

13 
PJM’s Manual 34 offers a useful high-level description of the interplay between the 
PJM stakeholder process and filing rights under Federal Power Act sections 205 and 206, 
as follows: 
Sections 205 and 206 of the Federal Power Act set forth the 
requirements that must be met to obtain FERC approval of a 
proposed revision to a governing document and are germane 
to the governing documents of PJM (the Operating 
Agreement, the Open Access Transmission Tariff (Tariff) and 
the Reliability Assurance Agreements (RAA)), and to the 
operation of the PJM stakeholder process. Sections 205 and 
206 establish the standards for demonstrating why a 
proposed revision to a governing document should be 
approved by the FERC. Section 205 requires that the 
proposer of a revision demonstrate the proposed revision is 
“just and reasonable.” Section 206 requires a potentially 
higher hurdle in that the proposer of a revision to the 
governing documents must demonstrate that the then current 
provisions are “unjust and unreasonable,” and that the 
proposed revisions are “just and reasonable.” Within the PJM 
stakeholder process it is recognized that the Members 
Committee maintains Section 205 authority over the 
Operating Agreement, and that the Board of Managers 
maintains Section 205 authority over the Open Access 
Transmission Tariff (Tariff) (with the exception of certain Tariff 
provisions that are under the exclusive control of the 
Transmission Owners) and the Reliability Assurance 
Agreements. Any party not possessing 205 authority over one 
of the governing documents may propose a revision to the 
document to the FERC under Section 206. It is also 
recognized that the Members provide input into the Regional 
Transmission Expansion Plan (“Plan”), and that the Plan is 
approved by the Board.11 
Manual 34 also describes the consultation process that PJM uses when making 
FPA section 205 filings. PJM is required under the Tariff to consult with the Transmission 
Owners and the MC at least seven days prior to filing. However, “neither the Transmission 
Owners, except as provided for in [Tariff] section 9.3, nor the PJM Members Committee 
 
11  PJM, Manual 34, Section 3, at 18.

14 
shall have any right to veto or delay any such Section 205 filing.”12 Further, “PJM may file 
with less than a full 7 day advance consultation in circumstances where imminent harm 
to system reliability or imminent severe economic harm to electric consumers requires a 
prompt Section 205 filing . . . .”13 
Question 6. Near-term Reforms 
 
What near-term reforms to stakeholder representation could PJM and its 
Members take to improve speed in decision-making while preserving stakeholder 
input? 
 
PJM needs to focus on issues related to reliability and resource adequacy above 
other issues. Stakeholders work on issues that require rapid development based on 
PJM’s meeting schedules. PJM sets the cadence for the stakeholder process through the 
calendar. PJM sets the priority of issues when it develops the calendar. If there is a 
concern about the speed of decision-making, that is not cause for reforming stakeholder 
representation. Instead, it only requires PJM to prioritize and schedule stakeholder 
meetings so key discussions can occur more quickly.  
Question 7. Committee Structure 
 
Are there elements of PJM’s committee structure that routinely contribute to 
delays?  Are there stakeholder processes or issues that could be expedited or 
changed to provide greater focus on key issues and allow faster or more 
unilateral action on others? 
 
As noted above, PJM controls the calendar, which sets the pace and prioritizes the 
issues; the committee structure is not the concern. Significantly, per Manual 34, “[t]he 
Secretary of the Members Committee has ultimate meeting prioritization decision.”14 
 
12  Id., Section 11.14, at 87. 
13  Id. 
14  Id., Section 11.4, at 80.

15 
Moreover, while the MC chair and vice chair are representatives of Members, the MC 
Secretary is a PJM staff member15 “appointed by the President of PJM,” who administers 
the stakeholder process procedures.16 The current MC Secretary is PJM’s Senior Director 
of Stakeholder Affairs.17 
Question 8. Expedited Action 
 
Should PJM increase the use of fast-path or time-bound review procedures to 
expedite committee action on high-importance topics?  
 
Simply scheduling additional meetings closer together to address mission-critical 
topics may be more effective than invoking truncated procedures. As we saw in the just 
completed CIFP-RBP/Connect & Manage process, when PJM attempts to use fast-path 
or time-bound review procedures to expedite action, PJM may trip itself up, resulting in 
wholesale changes to its own proposal. Similarly, stakeholders do not have sufficient time 
to work amongst themselves to consolidate their approaches, resulting in an unwieldy 
number of alternative proposals that often fail to consolidate into a clear consensus 
position. Further, expediting discussions in Valley Forge at the expense of consensus in 
the stakeholder process only serves to increase regulatory uncertainty. 
Question 9. Regional Differences 
 
Recognizing regional differences, are there lessons from other RTO/ISO 
stakeholder processes that PJM could reasonably adopt to improve speed in 
voting processes and stakeholder representation? 
 
When PJM’s stakeholders have time to thoroughly discuss an issue, understand 
one another’s opinions, and develop proposals that align with the theory of mutual gains 
 
15  See PJM, Members Committee, https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/committees/mc. 
16  PJM, Manual 34, Definitions (Secretary), at 16. 
17  See PJM, Members Committee, https://www.pjm.com/committees-and-groups/committees/mc.

16 
(the backbone of PJM’s Consensus Based Issues Resolution structure), the volume of 
proposals presented to the Members Committee is often greatly reduced, which in turn 
improves the speed at which the stakeholder process proceeds to a vote. While PJM’s 
stakeholder process is open to all interested parties, PJM’s stakeholders, including its 
Members, have very limited access to the PJM Board and essentially no insight into Board 
decisions on matters passed on by the Board that lead to a FERC filing (FPA sections 
205 or 206) until that decision is finalized, filed, and communicated via email to the 
stakeholders. The transparency improvements discussed supra in response to Question 
2 draw on MISO and SPP governance examples that suggest the PJM Board should 
provide more transparency regarding these matters.
